newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asia stocks mixed after Fed vote, seek direction.
newsitem.headline: Asia stocks mixed after Fed vote, seek direction.

text.p: Asia stock markets were mixed on Wednesday after the U.S. Federal Reserve decided to leave interest rates unchanged, sparking a sigh of relief among traders but little reaction.
Some markets shrugged off the news, focusing instead on local factors.
The outcome of the U.S. central bank's policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting on Tuesday ended a long-running guessing game on interest rates.
But the debate continues, with economists trying to guess the outcome of the next FOMC gathering on November 13.
"I'm cautiously optimistic," said Priscilla Ng, executive director and head of institutional sales at CEF GC Brokerage Ltd in Hong Kong.
"The trend suggests that there will be no need to raise U.S. interest rates in November either," she said.
The direction of U.S. interst rates is of particular interest to Hong Kong markets because the territory's currency, the Hong Kong dollar, is pegged to the U.S. dollar.
The key Hang Seng index gained half a percent, ending 56.83 points higher at 11,603.53.

Analysts saw the debate among Fed officials hinging on whether they would take a preemptive move against inflation by pushing interest rates higher or wait until there were clearer signs of an inflation build-up.
On Wall Street stocks rallied following news of the Fed's decision, but later retreated and ended off 20.71 points, or 0.35 percent, at 5,874.03.
Wall Street's uneasiness over the upcoming company results reporting season was evidenced by a 5-3/4 point drop in the stock of AT&T, which recently warned of an earnings shortfall.
In Tokyo, shares opened weak, but recovered to close higher amid strong buying in the semiconductor sector by large institutional investors.
"What led the market higher today were semiconductor-related shares," said a broker at a major Japanese securities house.
The key Nikkei 225 average gained 178.68 points, or 0.84 percent, to end at 21,350.67.
Early in the session traders said they were encouraged by the Fed's decision but that it would not prompt buying.

Elsewhere in Asia, South Korea's stocks advanced as investors bought blue chip stocks ahead of an October 1 regulation that will allow foreigners to buy up to 20 percent of most stocks, up from the current 18 percent.
The composite index ended 15.30 points, or 1.97 percent, higher, at 793.21.
Thai stocks remained pressured by concerns over the nomination of a new prime minister. At 0840GMT the SET index was off 11.00, or 1.06 percent, at 1,031.21.

Philippine shares closed 1.44 points, or 0.04 percent lower, at 3,235.04 as investors failed to be inspired by the Fed's decision. "The market has probably discounted the rate issue," Joey Roxas, president of Eagle Securities said in Manila.

Local investors gave a boost to Indonesian shares, which were up 1.39 points, or 0.24 percent, at 571.15, while speculative share buying helped bolster Malaysia's blue chip stocks. The composite index of blue chips shares was up 6.17 points, or 0.55 percent, at 1,129.89.
Singapore's Straits Times Index gained 4.05 points, or 0.19 percent, to 2,164.32, while Australia's All Ordinaries Index closed up 24.1 points, or 1.08 percent, at 2,252.8.
Taiwan closed lower ahead of a long weekend, with the weighted index off 39.33 points, or 0.61 percent, at 6,438.52.
